articles.text: The California Repercussions stage and marching band is set to return to Piedmont for its 58th annual Fourth of July Parade this Friday. The band will entertain parade-goers with classic and popular tunes alike. Based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the Repercussions are a 50-piece band made of equal parts brass, woodwinds, percussion, and party. For over 30 years the Repercussions have had the pleasure of playing for many discriminating clients and events such as the NFL Pro Bowl, the San Francisco Giants, the National Mayors’ Conference, and Oracle Corporation. The band has also thrilled crowds on international tours in London, Munich, Spain, Australia and Brazil. The band is composed of former college marching band members, primarily UC Davis, who may have graduated from school but never fully grew up. The Repercussions are known to have fun during their performances, waving horns in the air, dancing, and laughing their way along. Though the band is large, it promises not to be a constant wall of sound: the band mixes the power tunes in with others that feature a section of the band or a talented soloist. The California Repercussions will be marching in the Piedmont 4th of July Parade this year. Look for them as the final entry.

RELIGION CORNER Miracles and wonders By Dr. William McNabb Recently I had a successful heart ablation to correct Ventricular Tachycardia, an ailment I did not even realize I had until recently. At 8:00 a.m. I was wheeled into the Cath Lab at Summit Hospital in Oakland. At 3:00 p.m. the same day I was at home eating a hamburger. (The burger was not mentioned in the after-visit list of things to avoid.) This morning, I am reflecting on how this slow-motion miracle occurred. My cardiologist inserted electrodes on catheters into my groin and neck. They made their way to my heart where they had a Star Wars type light saber battle with a small spot on my ventricular wall that Darth Vader had taken over and was trying to lead a rebellion against my atria the rightful command central for my heart’s electrical signals. The entire war took place without my even knowing about it because of my excellent anesthesiologist, Dr. Yann. I have written before in previous hospital reports about how I was wonderfully taken care of by some nurses who all had uplifting Biblical names. Grace (unmerited forgiveness), Emmanuel (God with us), Angela (angel). They were immigrants from Nigeria, Eritrea and Mexico. This time my excellent nurses were Lan (China) and Raphael (Philippines). The brilliant general of this cardiac Star Wars battle was my cardiologist Dr. Rajan Shah from Iran. It is beyond tragic to think that if it were up to the vile Mr. Trump this man and those nurses may not have been welcomed in this country. I call what happened to me yesterday a slow-moving miracle. Perhaps it began in the 17th century when William Harvey, an English doctor, first described the circulatory system. Then discovery after discovery. I wonder what doctor first said, “maybe we can snake a wire through a vein into the heart and shock it into behaving correctly.” And what wonderful scientist invented these drugs that can put you to sleep instantly and wake you with no pain, grogginess or memory of what scary things just happened See Religion Corner on page 3 DICK CARTER, Florada Avenue Being in last year’s Piedmont parade with our Walking on Wednesdays group is one favorite. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council adopted a City budget for 2025- 2026 fiscal year at their regular meeting on Monday, June 16. The annual budget serves as a major policy document and describes how Piedmont intends to deliver its services and fund infrastructure in the coming year. The City’s $40.5 million General Fund budget includes the first year of new revenue from Measure F, a 20% increase in the Municipal Services Parcel Tax passed by voters in March 2023. Measure F funds will provide $538,000 in the coming year, which the City used to fund two additional 911 dispatch positions and an expansion of the Police Department’s automated license plate reader (ALPR) program. The FY2025-26 budget looks to maintain service levels citywide, prioritizing high quality service delivery, fiscal responsibility, and planning for the future while bringing several multi-year major projects to completion, including the City’s new community pool, the relocation of the 911 dispatch center, and the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Successful completion of the pool and dispatch center projects remain the City’s top priorities, followed by: • Installation of the Dearing Memorial at Triangle Park • Planning for a future public safety building to replace aging structures that do not meet modern standards for critical facilities. Additionally, next year’s budget focuses on investment in public spaces citywide. Capital improvements planned for the coming year include: • Repaving 1.9 miles of streets, re-striping an additional six miles of streets, and repairing 1,800 feet of sidewalk • New playground equipment at the Linda Beach Tot Lot and Piedmont Park • Upgrades to flood-prone storm drain infrastructure at eight locations across the city • Pathway repairs in Piedmont Park, similar to those recently completed at Crocker, Dracena, and Linda Parks • Four “DC fast charging” electric vehicle charging stations in the Civic Center Looking further ahead, the budget includes the development of a Sustainable Park Management Plan, identifying the management practices and future improvements needed to ensure Piedmont’s public spaces remain vibrant and support community needs long into the future. Adoption of the budget follows two City Council study sessions, review by the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, and two public hearings.

articles.text: Business owners can now apply for, renew, and pay annual tax for their City of Piedmont business license entirely online. The City’s new tool, launched in May, replaces a cumbersome paper-based process, providing community members a faster, simpler way to manage business licensing and rental taxes. Business owners no longer need to download forms, write checks, or visit City Hall in person. Through the new online portal, business owners can: • Apply for a new business license • Pay their annual business license tax, including rental business tax • Close their City of Piedmont business or rental account • Update contact information and business details All actions and payment history are stored in one place, accessible 24/7 from any device. Community members who need assistance using the online system can get help by calling a dedicated support number at (510) 250-1975 or by visiting City Hall, where staff can assist business owners with completing the process using the public online service kiosks located in the lobby. Licenses required for all businesses operating in Piedmont All businesses operating in Piedmont – including rental property owners – must have a valid business license. This includes, but is not limited to: • Home-based businesses (includes 1099 self-employment) • Online storefronts or “influencers” with a Piedmont business address • Landlords operating longterm or short-term rentals • Contractors and consultants working in Piedmont, even if located elsewhere Businesses that fail to obtain a license are subject to late fees and penalties. Learn more about licensing requirements and compliance at piedmont.ca.gov/BusinessCompliance. Part of a broader effort to modernize services The launch of online business licensing continues Piedmont’s work to make City business more accessible and user-friendly. This system joins the NextRequest public records portal, Piedmont Police CitizenConnect online incident map, and eTRAKiT online building and planning permit portal in a growing collection of digital services. Building on these efforts, a new City website is currently in development and scheduled to launch later this year.

City investing in public spaces The Piedmont City Council adopted a City budget for 2025- 2026 fiscal year at their regular meeting on Monday, June 16. The annual budget serves as a major policy document and describes how Piedmont intends to deliver its services and fund infrastructure in the coming year. The City’s $40.5 million General Fund budget includes the first year of new revenue from Measure F, a 20% increase in the Municipal Services Parcel Tax passed by voters in March 2023. Measure F funds will provide $538,000 in the coming year, which the City used to fund two additional 911 dispatch positions and an expansion of the Police Department’s automated license plate reader (ALPR) program. The FY2025-26 budget looks to maintain service levels citywide, prioritizing high quality service delivery, fiscal responsibility, and planning for the future while bringing several multi-year major projects to completion, including the City’s new community pool, the relocation of the 911 dispatch center, and the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Successful completion of the pool and dispatch center projects remain the City’s top priorities, followed by: • Installation of the Dearing Memorial at Triangle Park • Planning for a future public safety building to replace aging structures that do not meet modern standards for critical facilities. Additionally, next year’s budget focuses on investment in public spaces citywide. Capital improvements planned for the coming year include: • Repaving 1.9 miles of streets, re-striping an additional six miles of streets, and repairing 1,800 feet of sidewalk • New playground equipment at the Linda Beach Tot Lot and Piedmont Park • Upgrades to flood-prone storm drain infrastructure at eight locations across the city • Pathway repairs in Piedmont Park, similar to those recently completed at Crocker, Dracena, and Linda Parks • Four “DC fast charging” electric vehicle charging stations in the Civic Center Looking further ahead, the budget includes the development of a Sustainable Park Management Plan, identifying the management practices and future improvements needed to ensure Piedmont’s public spaces remain vibrant and support community needs long into the future. Adoption of the budget follows two City Council study sessions, review by the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, and two public hearings. articles.text: Piedmont Climate Fellow shines a light on what happens to plastic recyclables after the blue bin Ever wonder what happens to plastic after you put it in your blue recycling bin? The answer is more interesting than you might think. Piedmont’s recycling is sorted at Republic Services’ West County Resource Recovery Facility (WCRR) in Richmond. From there, plastics are bundled by type and sent out to be sold. The markets that accept different types of plastics constantly fluctuate. The types of plastic in highest demand are Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) – used for water bottles, soda bottles, and food containers – and High-Density Polyethylene (HDPE), commonly used for shampoo bottles, laundry detergent, and household cleaners. Republic Ser vices uses AI-powered arms to seamlessly identify PET plastic at its sorting facility, pulling out and bundling the most valuable plastics for shipment while ejecting other materials to avoid cross-contamination. These robots are currently being trained to collect HDPE plastics as well. For other types of plastic – often found in single use plastic bags, clamshells, packaging foam, and disposable drinking cups – recycling markets are more fluid. Even after placing these in a blue bin, likelihood of reprocessing may be slim and there’s a good chance they will find their way to a landfill. You can avoid the stress of wondering where these materials will end up by looking for ways to forgo them altogether. We call this strategy “stop or swap.” To “stop” is the act of eliminating a plastic good or material from your daily routine, opting for reusables instead. These can include stainless steel water bottles, tote bags, and reusable food containers. Where reusables aren’t an option, like when you’re buying milk at the grocery store, try to “swap.” Swap is the act of choosing plastics that have a stronger recycling market. For example, rather than purchasing milk in a carton, try to buy milk that comes in a glass bottle or #1 (PET) plastic jug. I want to close by reiterating that despite market fluidity, it is essential that as a community, we preserve our practices of placCity of Piedmont Climate Fellow Andrew Kaplowitz ing plastic goods in the blue bin. However, that isn’t to say we can’t implement change in our spending habits. Through the installation of stop and swap strategies, Piedmont can lower its environmental footprint by reducing the quantity of plastic that ends up in our landfills. If you are still unsure about how to dispose of waste and recyclables, StopWaste provides a tool called RE:Source, which is a search engine that allows you to input any type of item and see how it gets sorted in your community. articles.text: On March 4 this year Piedmont Unified School District said goodbye to two veteran Human Resource (HR) Managers, Kim Randlett and Suzanne Binder. Randlett has since been hired back in an elevated role as HR Director. On July 1 Randlett officially completed her first day in the new role which has many more responsibilities. Randlett had been handling contracts and HR details for all classified staff for 13 years and will now also be in charge of hiring and onboarding the other half of district contracts, those of teachers and certificated faculty. The school board brought her back after she applied for and officially secured the new job title on May 14. “Kim is just really the best. She is truly a rock star in terms of not only her expertise, but her skillset, and relationships with our staff,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. “She has such respect from all of our staff and it’s because she knows so much and really has a service attitude.” Randlett earned a degree in business from Webster University and holds a certificate from the ACSA Personnel Academy. Her Piedmont tenure began in 2007 as a Havens paraeducator. She moved into the district office in 2011 to support assistant superintendents Michael Brady and Randall Booker. The new role has 24 essential tasks. Randlett, well-respected within the district, will also be in charge of Title 9, administering grievance and disciplinary procedures for employees, and public record requests. Another new essential job responsibility for the Director will be as a liaison for union groups, and leading labor negotiations for PUSD. “I really pride myself on good relationships, my clear communication with staff and union leadership. I look forward to working with CSEA and APT the next coming school year. My door is always open, anytime anyone has any questions they can come anytime,” said Randlett in the May 14 board meeting. The Director will also take charge of job descriptions & salary schedules for district employees. The HR department will be augmented by an entry-level HR job under the Director, instead of having two managers. The job posting for the Payroll Technician II / Personnel Attendance role was posted June 25 at Edjoin.org/ Home/JobPosting/2107454 with an annual salary scale of $73,742- $90,648.

articles.text: Crucial—but often invisible—skills that let teenagers truly lift off A fledgling hawk’s wings look full long before it can soar. Hidden among the downy coverts are “primaries” and “secondaries”—the true flight feathers that bite the air and hold the bird aloft. Our kids, too, can appear ready for the big sky: decent grades, solid friendships, a résumé of clubs. Yet many stall once the thermals of late adolescence hit. Below are four less-obvious “feathers” parents can help cultivate—capacities that research links to stronger well-being and real-world traction. 1 Feedback Fluency Most teens dread criticism, yet the ability to seek and digest honest feedback predicts healthier self-concepts and lower depressive symptoms a year later. Coach your teen to ask three questions after any project—“What worked? What didn’t? What one change would have the biggest payoff?” Model the posture by soliciting their critique of your own decisions around the house. 2 Radical Responsibility & Clean Communication Blame feels lighter in the moment, but longitudinal data show that adolescents who practice taking full ownership for outcomes develop steadier social responsibility values in emerging adulthood. Pair that ownership with “clean” communication: when your head and your heart match your words and your actions. Having internal integrity in this way combined with seeking the lessons in challenging moments places cornerstones in the foundation of budding wisdom. 3 Expansive Curiosity Curiosity isn’t a trait; it’s an approach that can be trained. Teaching students the Question Formulation Technique boosted dispositional curiosity across an entire semester, which in turn lifted academic engagement. Help teens broaden and deepen their questioning by scheduling weekly “wonder walks”: 20-minute strolls where the only rule is to generate ten genuine questions about what they see or read. Curiosity widens the runway for future passions they can’t yet imagine. 4 Humble Collaboration Intellectual humility—the willingness to give up being right in order to stay connected— correlates with sharper critical thinking and more resilient relationships. Families can practice it with a simple ritual: in any debate, each side must restate the other’s viewpoint to their satisfaction before replying. The habit trains teens to treat disagreements as design sessions rather than zero-sum games. Take-Off Checklist (Next 30 Days) • Feedback Friday: over pizza, everyone shares one success and one improvement from • • • • the week. Ownership Ledger: teen logs daily instances of blame shifted and accepted; review patterns weekly. Question Jar: place a mason jar on the table; whoever contributes the most new questions in a week picks Friday’s dessert. Debate-and-Restate Night: choose a low-stakes topic (pineapple on pizza). Practice the humility ritual. Mentor Map: together, list five adults outside the family whom your teen trusts; draft a plan to ask one for feedback on a current goal. Why start now? Wisdom doesn’t appear when a driver’s license turns into a mortgage; it grows from thousands of small flights in safe airspace. By seeding feedback fluency, radical responsibility, expansive curiosity, and humble collaboration during the high-school years, you give your child the aerodynamic edge they’ll need when the winds pick up—and the confidence to leave the nest on their own power. Hidden among the downy coverts are “primaries” and “secondaries”—the true flight feathers that bite the air and hold the bird aloft. Our kids, too, can appear ready for the big sky: decent grades, solid friendships, a résumé of clubs. Yet many stall once the thermals of late adolescence hit. Below are four less-obvious “feathers” parents can help cultivate—capacities that research links to stronger well-being and real-world traction. 1 Feedback Fluency Most teens dread criticism, yet the ability to seek and digest honest feedback predicts healthier self-concepts and lower depressive symptoms a year later. Coach your teen to ask three questions after any project—“What worked? What didn’t? What one change would have the biggest payoff?” Model the posture by soliciting their critique of your own decisions around the house. 2 Radical Responsibility & Clean Communication Blame feels lighter in the moment, but longitudinal data show that adolescents who practice taking full ownership for outcomes develop steadier social responsibility values in emerging adulthood. Pair that ownership with “clean” communication: when your head and your heart match your words and your actions. Having internal integrity in this way combined with seeking the lessons in challenging moments places cornerstones in the foundation of budding wisdom. 3 Expansive Curiosity Curiosity isn’t a trait; it’s an approach that can be trained. Teaching students the Question Formulation Technique boosted dispositional curiosity across an entire semester, which in turn lifted academic engagement. Help teens broaden and deepen their questioning by scheduling weekly “wonder walks”: 20-minute strolls where the only rule is to generate ten genuine questions about what they see or read. Curiosity widens the runway for future passions they can’t yet imagine. 4 Humble Collaboration Intellectual humility—the willingness to give up being right in order to stay connected— correlates with sharper critical thinking and more resilient relationships. Families can practice it with a simple ritual: in any debate, each side must restate the other’s viewpoint to their satisfaction before replying. The habit trains teens to treat disagreements as design sessions rather than zero-sum games. Take-Off Checklist (Next 30 Days) • Feedback Friday: over pizza, everyone shares one success and one improvement from • • • • the week. Ownership Ledger: teen logs daily instances of blame shifted and accepted; review patterns weekly. Question Jar: place a mason jar on the table; whoever contributes the most new questions in a week picks Friday’s dessert. Debate-and-Restate Night: choose a low-stakes topic (pineapple on pizza). Practice the humility ritual. Mentor Map: together, list five adults outside the family whom your teen trusts; draft a plan to ask one for feedback on a current goal. Why start now? Wisdom doesn’t appear when a driver’s license turns into a mortgage; it grows from thousands of small flights in safe airspace. By seeding feedback fluency, radical responsibility, expansive curiosity, and humble collaboration during the high-school years, you give your child the aerodynamic edge they’ll need when the winds pick up—and the confidence to leave the nest on their own power. articles.text: St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland is partnering with the office of Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee to host a community Ceasefire Teach-In on Saturday, July 19, at the church on 114 Montecito Avenue. This neighborhood event is part of the Ceasefire Teach-In Series, an initiative by Mayor Lee and her Public Safety Working Group to engage local communities in meaningful dialogue about ending gun violence in Oakland. Speakers will include Mayor Lee, Oakland Police Chief Floyd Mitchell, and Violence Prevention Chief Dr. Holly Joshi, along with other public safety leaders. Together, they will describe the data, strategies, and evolution of Oakland’s Ceasefire program. “We are deeply committed to peace and justice in our community,” said the Rev. Dr. Mauricio Wilson, rector of St. Paul’s Episcopal Church. “We are grateful for the opportunity to host this vital conversation and invite all of our neighbors to join us.” RSVPs are encouraged at bit.ly/OaklandMayorCeasefireTeachIn or by email to ddaavis-howard@oaklandca.gov. articles.text: Staff Photos Aubrey Turner, PHS Class of 2020, appeared with Oakland Soul in its W League season. Aubrey Turner graduated from Piedmont High in 2020, signing on with the University of Portland to play Division 1 collegiate soccer. Now five years since she graced the halls of PHS, Turner returned to the Bay Area to play professionally for Oakland Soul of the USL W League. “It’s a surreal feeling to walk out on the pitch for a home game and to see the number of fans Soul has. It shows how Oakland has always cared about its teams and always comes out strong,” Turner said. Although she only appeared once for Soul before aggravating an injury, Turner was able to get back on the field and train with the club. “I started training with Soul in March and right before our first game, I hurt my ankle. I have a history of ankle injuries, so that told me I need to take time to get healthy if I want to continue playing,” Turner explained. After concluding her collegiate career with the Pilots in the fall of 2023, Turner traveled to Europe to play professionally with F.C. Famalicã, a team in the top tier of Portuguese football and located in the northern Portugal city of Vila Nova de Famalicão. With the help of an agent, Turner landed a workout at F.C. Famalicão and impressed their coaching staff enough to earn a roster spot. “It was December 2023 and I was deciding on whether to use my fifth year or play professionally. I was put in touch with an agent and I went on trial with Famalicão. They were interested in me and that’s how I wound up in Portugal,” Turner said of her time in Portugal. In 2024, Turner had four appearances at Famalicão for a total of 84 minutes. “I always wanted to live abroad and I was able to do that outside of soccer. Playing just 30 minutes away from the city of Porto, some of Aubrey’s favorite memories were watching her favorite team, Arsenal, play FC Porto in the Champions League and, of course, eating delectable Portuguese food. “Portugal itself is beautiful, I want to go back. The food is amazing; I’m still trying to find a good natas place out here. I went to a Porto vs. Arsenal game, that was fun to just watch the fan base environment out there. The fans are screaming and singing nonstop. They know every chant and sway back and forth,” Turner said. JACK STEIN Cross County, Track & Field Piedmont High Class of 2022 Pomona-Pitzer Class of 2026 Jack Stein, PHS Class of 2022, just finished his junior year on Pomona-Pitzer’s cross country and track teams. In cross country last fall, he finished the season by helping his school place third of 32 teams in the Division 3 NCAA Championship on November 23. Stein finished the race 28th of 294 athletes with a time of 24:34.3 on the 8K course. Stein also competed in track in the 5K and 10K events at the SCAIC Track and Field Championship on April 26-27. He finished the 5K seventh of 44 runners with a time of 14:57.80. He was second of 16 runners in the 10K, clocking a 30:57.88. As a sophomore, Stein helped the Sagehens claim the 2023 Division 3 NCAA Championship by defeating Wisconsin La Crosse by just one point, 158-159, where the former Highlanders’ star finished as Pitzer’s fifth-best runner—meaning his time of 25:49.3 was what they ultimately needed to win the title. Stein graduated from Piedmont High as its All-Time record holder in the 1600 and 3200 meters with respective times of 4:14.77 and 9:12.62. I plan how many miles I want to run on a weekly basis and track them on Strava. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? articles.text: Visit the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco on Sunday, July 6 for a film screening of Disney’s Mulan followed by a family-friendly magazine workshop and collection tour. Mulan, based on the Chinese legend of Hua Mulan, broke new ground as a Disney film when it premiered in 1998. Fa Mulan, the protagonist, became the first Disney princess of East Asian descent and was conceived by animators and writers as more of a warrior-heroine than a princess. Variety’s Todd McCarthy praised the character at the time for inspiring “a turn of the circle from such age-old Disney classics ... in which passive heroines were rescued by blandly noble princes.” The museum will host a screening and singalong of Mulan in Samsung Hall at 11:30 a.m. The screening will be followed by a ‘Zine’ lesson suitable for children ages 6 to 16 in the Koret Education Center. Tours will be held throughout the day, including a docent tour of Yuan GoangMing: Everyday War at 11 a.m., and a collection tour at 2 p.m. The event is part of the museum’s Free First Sunday, where museum admission is free and visitors are encouraged to enjoy cultural celebrations, hands-on workshops, live dance and music performances, food pop-ups and tastings, and other community events, as well as the museum’s world-renowned collection and special exhibitions. articles.text: Legion of Honor, one of the Fine Arts museums of San Francisco, is currently exhibiting more than 250 personal photographs by Paul McCartney in a never-before seen collection entitled Paul McCartney: Photographs 1963–64: Eyes of the Storm through July. The exhibition includes the Beatles’ songwriter and singer personal captures as well as video clips, archival materials and more that offer a behind-the-scenes look at the meteoric rise of one of the world’s most celebrated and popular bands. Images span December 1963 through February 1964 and chronicle the Beatles’ journey to megastardom. Photographs were taken by McCartney with a single-lens reflex camera, which were introduced in the 1950’s as part of a new generation of handheld cameras. Sally Martin Katz, Legion of Honor Assistant Curator of Photography, said that McCartney acquired the camera in 1963 at a time “when many were experimenting with this newly popularized medium.” “The technology of the 35mm handheld camera allowed for a spontaneity in picture-taking, leading to the emergence of a snapshot aesthetic that embraced imperfection,” Katz said. “McCartney’s pictures reflect this new spirit in photography, as well as the literal blur of travel that The Beatles were experiencing, rapidly moving from one place to another.” Katz added that the exhibition, which includes photographs printed for the first time, captures “Beatlemania in full force.” “They depict the frenzied crowds chasing the band down the New York City streets, for example, and the swarms of people greeting them at the Miami airport,” she said. “The Beatles were at the eye of the storm they created: thousands of eyes were looking to capture that storm, and McCartney, with his camera, returned their gazes.” Visit https://www.famsf.org/ exhibitions/paul-mccartney-photographs to learn more. articles.text: Paul Simon American singer-songwriter Paul Simon, who rose to fame in the 1960’s as part of the folk-rock duo Simon & Garfunkel, will perform three concerts at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco July 19, 21 and 22 as part of his “Quiet Celebration” spring and summer tour. The legendary artist and Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductee wrote the duo’s hits, including “Bridge Over Troubled Water,” “Mrs. Robinson,” before embarking on his own successful solo career in 1971. Simon’s “Quiet Celebration” tour, his first since 2018, features the live debut of his Grammy-nominated album, Seven Psalms, along with a celebration of his timeless classics. Simon has contended with severe hearing loss and has chosen intimate venues with optimal acoustics for this tour, his team said in a statement. The band traveling with Simon includes talented musicians such as Caleb Burhans, Jamey Haddad, Gyan Riley, Mick Rossi, Andy Snitzer, Nancy Stagnitta, Mark Stewart, Eugene Friesen, Steve Gadd, and Matt Chamberlain. The San Francisco Symphony does not appear in the concerts at Davies Symphony Hall. Simon recently cancelled his June 28 and 29 shows scheduled at Philadelphia’s Academy of Music following “chronic and intense back pain.” “Today it became unmanageable and demands immediate attention,” reads a statement on Simon’s social media account Instagram. “Unfortunately we have to cancel these shows at this time, as we don’t have the ability to reschedule them.” The post continued, “However, we are hopeful after this minor surgical procedure which has been scheduled in the next few days, Paul will be able to complete the tour as well as look into returning to make up these dates.” Tickets can be purchased by visiting https://www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2024-25/ Paul-Simon. Ticket-holders may be entitled to refunds if San Francisco shows are cancelled.

articles.text: The iconic Fillmore Jazz Festival returns to San Francisco for its 36th year on July 5 and 6. Fillmore Jazz Festival is the West Coast’s largest free, ongoing jazz festival. The event attracts more than 50,000 attendees annually, and spans twelve blocks on Fillmore from Jackson to Eddy with two main stages at California and Eddy. Select performances are held inside the Calvary Presbyterian Church and Jones Memorial United Methodist Church. This year’s theme is “Lift Every Voice,” drawing inspiration from the famous hymn based on the poem by NAACP leader James Weldon Johnson in 1900. “Lift Every Voice and Sing” was first performed by schoolchildren in celebration of Abraham Lincoln’s birthday and over time became a rallying cry during the Civil Rights Movement. Today it remains a powerful symbol of Black pride, perseverance, and hope and was referred to as the Black national anthem by the NAACP. Fillmore Jazz Festival’s 36th engagement features an eclectic lineup across multiple music venues, showcasing the talents of more than 25 local and nationally-renowned artists. The festival also offers more than 140 arts and crafts booths, 25 food vendors and face painting and activities for kids. The event is free and no registration is required. The festival begins at 10 a.m. and ends at 6 p.m. both Saturday, July 5 and Sunday, July 6. Visit https:// www.fillmorejazzfest.com to learn more.
articles.title: Fillmore Jazz Festival returns to San Francisco July 5-6

articles.text: Valley of the Moon Music Festival kicks off its 11th season in Sonoma County, entitled “Liaisons,” on July 12. Valley of the Moon will present ten concerts that highlight historical instruments, offering guests a rare opportunity to enjoy classical music as originally intended. Valley of the Moon is nestled in the heart of Sonoma County’s wine country and brings together new artists, world-renowned classically trained musicians and music lovers in intimate settings. Each concert at the Hanna Center Auditorium in Sonoma County is followed by a complimentary wine reception. Tolling is an internationally renowned violinist and composer, a two-time Grammy award-winner, and the 2016 DownBeat Critics Poll Rising Star winner. He is best known for his work with the Turtle Island Quartet, Stanley Clarke, Bob Weir, and local groups including the all-star San Francisco String Trio. articles.text: Materialized Thoughts, and art exhibit currently on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, brings together Nepali artists living in the USA as first-generation immigrants. The body of works displayed explores the paradoxes of diasporic life, particularly the process of building identity amid pressures to conform to dominant cultures and homogeneous identities. Drawing inspiration from everyday life and personal experiences, this exhibition reflects the tension between strong attachment to the culture left behind and the process of assimilating into a new society. These artworks investigate the nuanced realities of diasporic life – living “in between” cultures, constantly navigating the differences and similarities between homeland and host land, and the ongoing process of carving out a new identity. The themes of “double-consciousness” – being “here and there” at the same time. This exhibition is the culmination of the research on Nepali Diaspora Artists based in the Bay Area and beyond, conducted by Swosti Rajbhandari Kayastha as a Fulbright Visiting Scholar with the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. The research was conducted over seven months from November 2024 to June 2025. This exhibition is the first of its kind, featuring artworks selectively by Diaspora Nepali Artists, showcasing diverse cultural narratives, challenging dominant art world narratives, and fostering dialogue about identity, displacement, and belonging. This exhibition has provided a platform for artists to express their unique experiences and perspectives, often highlighting the complexities of navigating multiple cultures and identities, seeking to play a crucial role in cultural preservation, documentation of history, and promoting cross-cultural understanding. Through such exhibitions by diaspora artists, you can help gain a deeper understanding of cultural identity, witness artistic innovation, and engage with important social issues. They also foster empathy and understanding of shared human experiences, challenges, and triumphs, providing an opportunity to celebrate the diversity of artistic talent and contribute to a more inclusive art world. Supporting diaspora artists can contribute to a more inclusive and globally oriented art world enriching the cultural landscape and contribute to a broader understanding of the diaspora’s impact on contemporary culture and society.

pages.text: 18 18 Wednesday, July 2, 2025 Nepali art exhibit in Piedmont Materialized Thoughts, and art exhibit currently on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, brings together Nepali artists living in the USA as first-generation immigrants. The body of works displayed explores the paradoxes of diasporic life, particularly the process of building identity amid pressures to conform to dominant cultures and homogeneous identities. Drawing inspiration from everyday life and personal experiences, this exhibition reflects the tension between strong attachment to the culture left behind and the process of assimilating into a new society. These artworks investigate the nuanced realities of diasporic life – living “in between” cultures, constantly navigating the differences and similarities between homeland and host land, and the ongoing process of carving out a new identity. The themes of “double-consciousness” – being “here and there” at the same time. This exhibition is the culmination of the research on Nepali Diaspora Artists based in the Bay Area and beyond, conducted by Swosti Rajbhandari Kayastha as a Fulbright Visiting Scholar with the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. The research was conducted over seven months from November 2024 to June 2025. This exhibition is the first of its kind, featuring artworks selectively by Diaspora Nepali Artists, showcasing diverse cultural narratives, challenging dominant art world narratives, and fostering dialogue about identity, displacement, and belonging. This exhibition has provided a platform for artists to express their unique experiences and perspectives, often highlighting the complexities of navigating multiple cultures and identities, seeking to play a crucial role in cultural preservation, documentation of history, and promoting cross-cultural understanding. Through such exhibitions by diaspora artists, you can help gain a deeper understanding of cultural identity, witness artistic innovation, and engage with important social issues. They also foster empathy and understanding of shared human experiences, challenges, and triumphs, providing an opportunity to celebrate the diversity of artistic talent and contribute to a more inclusive art world. Supporting diaspora artists can contribute to a more inclusive and globally oriented art world enriching the cultural landscape and contribute to a broader understanding of the diaspora’s impact on contemporary culture and society. articles.text: Roy Scheider and Robert Shaw in Jaws The now iconic film Jaws was released on 464 screens simultaneously on June 20, 1975. It was the No.1 film in America for 14 weeks and went on to generate three sequels. The story, set on a quiet New England tourist island called Amity, finds its primal sweet spot in the first harrowing scene and never relents. Its late at night and we see a teenage beach party underway. A girl and boy are flirting, he’s drinking, and when he approaches her, she impulsively gets up and runs toward the water, leaving him and her clothes behind. She dives into the darkness of the ocean and begins to swim slowly out toward a ringing navigation buoy, pausing only to tread water. The only sound is the hollow clang of the bell until we hear the soft yet ominous background score of John Williams. The girl, having reached the buoy holds onto it and suddenly her calm face grimaces and then is frozen in fear and terror. Her boyfriend, now standing near the water, unaware, calls out to her. The audience watches as she is lifted and pushed through the water, terrified, and suddenly is pulled beneath the surface. That riveting moment frames the entire narrative, reminding the audience that below the all but flat and seemingly benign surface of the waves is an unseen lethal presence. The grim remains of the young woman are discovered the following morning, and the Amity Police Chief, Martin Brody (Roy Schieder), is called to investigate. articles.text: The film If Beale Street Could Talk opens with a quotation from author James Baldwin: “Beale Street is a street in New Orleans where my father and Louis Armstrong were born. As was jazz. Every black person in America was born on Beale Street, whether in Jackson, Mississippi, or in Harlem, New York. Beale Street is our legacy.” And it is that legacy that writer-director Barry Jenkins (Moonlight) explores, his film a painful and aspirational adaptation of Baldwin’s 1974 novel. As well, it makes explicit that Beale Street is not so much a street but a remarkable metaphor for a life experience, viewed through the prism of what it means to be black in America. The film opens with Tish (Kiki Layne), 19, and Fonny (Stephan James), 22, walking through a park. Immediately it is clear that they are deeply in love. In voice over, Tish explains that they have been friends since childhood and with age their connection has changed, morphing into an all encompassing love while they move ever so cautiously toward consummating their feelings and making love. As Tish explains, this is the world they move in and so profound is their attachment that it’s as if they possess a luminescent halo that surrounds them, one defined by hope and joy. Watching them standing together, embracing, foreheads touching, it’s obvious that Beale Street is a deeply emotive love story. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Coco The story of Coco follows a 12-year-old boy named Miguel Rivera (Anthony Gonzalez) who lives in the small Mexican town of Cecilia. He dreams of one day becoming a musician, exactly like the legendary Ernesto De La Cruz (Benjamin Bratt), an iconic guitar player. Miguel secretly practices while studying video footage of Ernesto. There is, however, a problem, and it is not a small one: the Riveras are shoemakers. They are part of the artisan trade community, and theirs is a tradition that has been proudly passed along from one generation to the next. The expectation is that Miguel will be what the Rivera men were before him, shoemakers. Music playing is strictly forbidden. Meanwhile, Miguel yearns to participate in a talent show to be held in the town plaza on the Dia De Muertas, a day when those who are deceased visit the living. His ancient great grandmother, Coco (Ana Ofelia Marguia), the strict matriarch of the Rivera family, and the daughter of Miguel’s great-great grandmother, Imelda, sternly supports the family’s ban on music playing. In preparation for the Dia De Muertas, the Riveras have created an elaborate shrine with the photos of deceased family members. Miguel, if he going to be in the talent show, realizes he will need a guitar. He goes to the tomb of Ernesto and there finds his guitar, which he steals. At that quirky moment Miguel is transported to the Land of the Dead and it is there that he meets all of his past relatives who are preparing for their journey on this very special day. When he meets up with his great-great grandmother, Imelda (Alana Ubach), she makes it clear that he must quit music. Of course, she has a dark history with musicians. During his adventure, Miguel hooks up with a scallywag called Hector (Gael Garcia Bernal), and also has a sidekick, a spifffy dog. There is one caveat to Miguel’s family reunion with those who have passed away, and that is he must return to the Land of the Living by dawn or he will remain forever in the Land of the Dead. All he needs is a blessing from a deceased relative. And so, his journey continues. This is a beautifully animated feature film, one of Pixar’s best, filled with vibrant colors, cultural themes, wonderful songs, and amazing alebrijes (folk art sculptures). Of course, the embedded importance of family runs throughout the story, as well as the importance of following your dreams, all of it leading Miguel to finding peace in the Land of the Living. Coco. Directed by Lee Unkrich. Pixar/Disney Animation. Starring Anthony Gonzalez, Gael Garcia Bernal, Benjamin Bratt. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Released in 2017. Now streaming on Disney+/Prime/Fandango. articles.text: The Eagle Huntress, set in the stark Altai Mountains of the Mongolian steppes, is, in so many ways, extraordinary. When commenting on the vast, isolated plains and unforgiving snow-covered mountains, director Otto Bell said, “It’s not the end of the world, but you can see it from there.” This breathtaking film is intermittently narrated by Daisy Ridley in English, with subtitles. The sweeping cinematography, by Simon Niblett, is gorgeous, at times involving a drone for aerial shots of eagles in flight, their grace and beauty something to behold. But at the center of this beautifully rendered documentary is a 13-year-old girl, Aisholpan Nurgaiv, who explains to her father, Nurgaiv, that she wishes to follow him in what is a centuries old tradition. She wants above all to become an eagle huntress. He tells Aisholpan that for generations only men have been allowed to use eagles to hunt small game for fur and meat. She has heard of the annual Golden Eagle competition and appeals to her father to let her train an eagle and enter the contest. Of course, the tribe’s council of elders opines about a young woman, a girl, actually, joining the 70 other hunters who will arrive in the provincial capital of Olgii to compete. Women, they insist, are too fragile and lack the stamina and strength to hunt with raptors, birds that can stand almost three feet tall, with wingspans of six feet or more. But Nurgaiv encourages his daughter, who is hardworking, ever cheerful, unexpectedly intrepid and resolutely committed to becoming the first female eagle huntress. And so, with the help of her father, who is a gentle and supportive coach and clearly cares deeply about his child, they set out to find and capture an eaglet, one still in its nest, somewhere high in a mountain crevice. What is remarkable about this journey on horseback is not only the effort by Aisholpan, as she rappels down a fissure with her father high above on belay, but the nature of their interaction. Of course, the tribe’s council of elders opines about a young woman, a girl, actually, joining the 70 other hunters who will arrive in the provincial capital of Olgii to compete. Women, they insist, are too fragile and lack the stamina and strength to hunt with raptors, birds that can stand almost three feet tall, with wingspans of six feet or more. But Nurgaiv encourages his daughter, who is hardworking, ever cheerful, unexpectedly intrepid and resolutely committed to becoming the first female eagle huntress. And so, with the help of her father, who is a gentle and supportive coach and clearly cares deeply about his child, they set out to find and capture an eaglet, one still in its nest, somewhere high in a mountain crevice. What is remarkable about this journey on horseback is not only the effort by Aisholpan, as she rappels down a fissure with her father high above on belay, but the nature of their interaction. Nurgaiv encourages, always kind, and Aisholpan perseveres. He dreams of one day becoming a musician, exactly like the legendary Ernesto De La Cruz (Benjamin Bratt), an iconic guitar player. Miguel secretly practices while studying video footage of Ernesto. There is, however, a problem, and it is not a small one: the Riveras are shoemakers. They are part of the artisan trade community, and theirs is a tradition that has been proudly passed along from one generation to the next. The expectation is that Miguel will be what the Rivera men were before him, shoemakers. Music playing is strictly forbidden. Meanwhile, Miguel yearns to participate in a talent show to be held in the town plaza on the Dia De Muertas, a day when those who are deceased visit the living. His ancient great grandmother, Coco (Ana Ofelia Marguia), the strict matriarch of the Rivera family, and the daughter of Miguel’s great-great grandmother, Imelda, sternly supports the family’s ban on music playing. In preparation for the Dia De Muertas, the Riveras have created an elaborate shrine with the photos of deceased family members. Miguel, if he going to be in the talent show, realizes he will need a guitar. He goes to the tomb of Ernesto and there finds his guitar, which he steals. At that quirky moment Miguel is transported to the Land of the Dead and it is there that he meets all of his past relatives who are preparing for their journey on this very special day. When he meets up with his great-great grandmother, Imelda (Alana Ubach), she makes it clear that he must quit music. Of course, she has a dark history with musicians. During his adventure, Miguel hooks up with a scallywag called Hector (Gael Garcia Bernal), and also has a sidekick, a spifffy dog. There is one caveat to Miguel’s family reunion with those who have passed away, and that is he must return to the Land of the Living by dawn or he will remain forever in the Land of the Dead. All he needs is a blessing from a deceased relative. And so, his journey continues. This is a beautifully animated feature film, one of Pixar’s best, filled with vibrant colors, cultural themes, wonderful songs, and amazing alebrijes (folk art sculptures). Of course, the embedded importance of family runs throughout the story, as well as the importance of following your dreams, all of it leading Miguel to finding peace in the Land of the Living. Coco. Walkers view design award winners By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group is not surprised when unexpected, happy things happen on their walks of Piedmont streets. Last Wednesday some serendipitous encounters added significantly to their walk enjoyment. There was a large turnout of 55 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra for the fun. To be eligible, a project must conform to Piedmont’s design and planning guidelines and must have completed construction in the previous calendar year. The first home for the walkers to see was the winner of the Excellence in Comprehensive Remodel with Integrated Accessory Dwelling Unit at 224 Greenbank Avenue. By coincidence, David Lee, the homeowner, was outside working. After introductions, David told the group about his project. The house’s footprint had to stay the same, so the crawlspace at the house’s front was cleared and used for more room and an ADU. New windows matched existing ones and solar and a heat pump were part of the project. The neighbors were supportive of the effort. It took one year, but David said he was glad they did it and would do it again. After thanking David, the walkers went down to Grand Avenue, up Cambridge Way, and over to York Drive. The next destination was 47 York Drive and on the way there was another house to see – the home of Piedmont realtor Stacey Isaacs and Chuck Wolf. As the walkers approach the now complete, modern, beautiful house, they had their second happy surprise of the morning. Stacey had seen them coming, came out to welcome them, and shared the project’s story. Stacey and Chuck bought the original house six years ago. They liked that the lot was deep and level and intended to remodel the house. Some projects were started but they came to realize that to have the house the way they wanted, it would be better to take the old house down and start all over. That’s what they did. They first built an ADU to live in during the two years of new house construction. The project took more time and money than they had expected, but the house is spectacular. After sharing the history, Stacey provided the group’s third surprise of the morning. She generously invited the 55 walkers to come inside. It was an offer they couldn’t refuse. The home is an open-concept jewel. It’s beautifully detailed and furnished and flows nicely from the front to the backyard with the ADU on the side and a raised swimming pool of a modern designed at the back. The walkers greatly enjoyed Stacey’s open house and had to be reminded that there was another house to see on the block. Thanks were given to Stacey and Chuck for their hospitality and group made their way up to 47 York. This house was the winner for Excellence in for a Second Story Addition. The walkers enjoyed seeing the seamlessly added second floor to the house. It was a good thing property owners Kevin Ma and Liana Wu were not there to talk about their project because the unexpected and happy visits with David, Stacey, and Chuck had taken a good piece of the morning. There wasn’t time to go up to Estrella Avenue and see James Glauber and Tracy Lieu’s City Sustainability Award winner on Estrella Avenue. It would have to be part of a future Wednesday walk. The group retraced their steps back York to Cambridge and then returned to the Exedra via, Blair, San Carlos, Oakland, El Cerrito, and Magnolia Avenues. The walkers should have expected it was another walk of surprises and fun. But his real passion was advertising. His career began at Guild, Bascom & Bonfigli, a storied firm of its day, where he worked as a graphic designer, followed by a stint at Dancer Fitzgerald Sample. In 1968, John became creative director at San Francisco’s Aviva Toy Company, which produced toys based on Charles Schulz’s beloved Peanuts comic strip. A dog lover and gifted illustrator, John played a central role in bringing Snoopy off the page and into the physical world, shaping Schulz’s iconic beagle into toys and merchandise that became part of daily life for millions. In 1977, John opened his own agency, The Design Bunch, specializing in print advertising and design. He moved to Piedmont and commuted to work from Oakland by ferry, accompanied by his dog du jour. After 50 productive years, John retired in 2015, celebrating the occasion with a grand party in Alsace, France. In 1992, he enrolled in evening classes at Piedmont Adult School, and five years later, one of his golf paintings was selected for the official poster and program cover of the AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am Golf Tournament. The honor made John a mini-celebrity and gave him the chance to mix with the likes of Clint Eastwood and Kevin Costner, just a few of the tournament’s many high-profile guests. John went on to specialize in painting golf courses, landscapes, and, most notably, dog portraits. A lifelong dog lover, he considered those portraits family treasures. But his subject range was much larger. I remember a delightful portrait of Queen Elizabeth that John painted for her jubilee, which hung above his mantelpiece. His dining room table was always piled with sketches and drying watercolors. John was also known among California car enthusiasts as the owner of a 1954 powder-blue Jaguar XK 120 convertible. Quite possibly the classiest car ever made, it had been driven by the likes of Clark Gables, Humphrey Bogart and Frank Sinatra, and earned John numerous awards, including several at car shows hosted by Piedmont. He once took me for a spin in his immaculately maintained treasure, its brilliant blue the color of California sky. We drove to Orinda, drawing enthusiastic honks at intersections and turning quite a few heads. Held in my passenger seat by a rough airplane-grade seat belt, I felt like a Hollywood star riding beside a Bogart-style dandy – aviator glasses, bright neck scarf, and leather gloves to match his jacket – at least until the Jaguar lost power climbing a steep hill. Beyond the Wildlife Confiscations Network, Oakland Zoo has played a crucial role in rescuing and caring for a diverse range of animals, including insects, amphibians, primates, and birds. Since 2021, the Oakland Zoo has received over 100 requests from wildlife agencies, advocacy groups, and animal rescue organizations for assistance with rescue efforts. These efforts aim to support victims of the wildlife pet trade, roadside zoos, and other criminal activities. “With Oakland Zoo’s decadelong history of animal rescue and efforts to end the wildlife trade, it is essential to continually expand the Zoo’s role in combating this tragic industry. We are proud to be part of the Wildlife Confiscations Network, which has united our efforts toward a common mission and offers us a new opportunity to help save more wildlife that are victims of trafficking,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. Funding for the position is provided by the CDFW and is focused primarily on requests for triage and temporary holding of trafficked or illegally held animals within the state of California. This role is distinct from the Zoo’s other wildlife rescue programs.
